evidence.question: 3. What are the documented medical benefits for the newborn of delayed cord clamping (e.g., increased iron stores, improved circulation)?
evidence.answer: The search result documents several medical benefits of delayed cord clamping for newborns. Delayed cord clamping can increase the baby's blood volume by up to 33%, which provides significant health advantages. First, it **increases iron stores**: the extra blood from delayed clamping gives newborns a supplemental iron boost, ensuring sufficient iron to fuel rapid growth and development, since breastmilk alone cannot provide all the iron newborns need. Notably, "one clinical study found that 4-year-old children who had delayed cord clamping at birth had higher cognitive and motor scores compared to peers whose cords were immediately clamped." Second, it **improves brain myelin levels**: a 2018 study in *The Journal of Pediatrics* found that a 5-minute delay in clamping results in increased myelin—a white fatty substance that coats and insulates nerve connections in the brain, leading to more efficient brain development. The World Health Organization has consequently recommended delayed cord clamping in all births, advising that clamping "should not be done until at least 1-3 minutes after delivery or longer."

retrieval.text:
During the last 3 months of pregnancy, antibodies from mothers are passed to their unborn babies through the placenta.
This type of immunity is called passive immunity because the baby has been given antibodies rather than making them itself.
Antibodies are special proteins the immune system produces to help protect the body against bacteria and viruses.
The amount and type of antibodies passed to the baby depends on the mother's immunity.
For example, if you have had chickenpox, you should have developed immunity against the condition and some of the chickenpox antibodies will be passed to your baby.
But if you haven't had chickenpox, your baby will not be protected.
Immunity in newborn babies is only temporary and starts to decrease after the first few weeks or months.
Breast milk also contains antibodies, which means that babies who are breastfed have passive immunity for longer.
The thick yellowish milk (colostrum) produced for the first few days following birth is particularly rich in antibodies.
Premature babies are at higher risk of developing an illness because their immune systems are not as strong and they haven't had as many antibodies passed to them.
